1:
Calvin (reformed) opens with the objection the chapter invites: it might look as though God had given an imperfect law of succession, and had not thought of this difficulty until the chief men raised it. His answer is that the earlier ruling secured the rights of individuals and this one treats the general advantage or loss, and that God so arranged his replies that he assigned each party its rights only when he was asked. The daughters came and demanded justice and were heard; now the heads of the tribe come and press the loss they would suffer, and provision is made that no other tribe be enriched at their expense. He adds the point that keeps it from being a quarrel: this is not one question breeding another while each side pushes its own interest, for when God takes cognizance of the matter he pronounces that both parties asked only what was right.

Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads the approach as a model of how to bring a grievance. The petitioners belong to the half of Manasseh that has not yet received its lot west of Jordan, and yet they speak of the land of their possession and the inheritance of their fathers as confidently as if it were already in hand, knowing whom they had trusted. They recite the earlier order fairly and do not ask to have it set aside, since none of them knows but that his own family may one day need it. Gill (reformed) identifies them as the princes of Manasseh, the tribe descended from Gilead. Both Henry and Gill suspect the petition was prompted by something concrete rather than a hypothetical: young men of other tribes were already paying court to these heiresses, with an eye to enlarging their own inheritance. Henry will not let that pass without comment, that in making marriages the convenience of the estate is aimed at more than it should be, and the meetness of the person less.

Calvin states the petitioners’ argument as a clash of two laws. The land was to be distributed by lot at God’s command; if women carry their tribe’s inheritance elsewhere, the lots fall into confusion. They take it as beyond question that God cannot be inconsistent with himself, so what is needed is an interpretation that removes the contradiction, and in asking for one they submit to his governance rather than disputing it. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) makes a proposal about the text rather than the law: this chapter and the first eleven verses of Numbers 27 are parts of one subject, and either that passage belongs before this chapter or this chapter belongs immediately after it. He states the ruling in a sentence — heiresses marry within their own tribe, so that no part of the ancient inheritance is alienated from the original family.

What the jubilee does here divides the witnesses three ways. The petitioners appeal to it as the moment the loss becomes final, and Ellicott (grammatical-historical) agrees, adding what makes the appeal intelligible: until the jubilee the inheritance might still return to Manasseh, by purchase or if the marriages proved childless, and the jubilee is what makes the transfer permanent. Gill takes it further and turns the institution against itself. Restoring inheritances to their original proprietors is no help in this case but rather the reverse, since it would fix the daughters’ portions in the tribes they had married into; and he cites Jewish commentators who read the clause concessively, that though a jubilee comes it will be no advantage. Keil (grammatical-historical) corrects the premise of the whole complaint: strictly the property would pass to the husband’s tribe at the marriage itself, not at the jubilee Leviticus 25:10 appoints. On his reading the petitioners have named the wrong date for a loss that is real enough.
5:
The answer opens with an endorsement, and Henry (puritan-evangelical) makes much of it: the tribe of the sons of Joseph hath said well. Those who consult the oracles of God about securing an inheritance are not only answered but have their enquiry accepted, receiving a well said as well as a well done. Two witnesses notice that the text never says Moses took the case to God. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) points out that in the daughters’ earlier application it was stated expressly that he brought their cause before the LORD at Numbers 27:5, and that the phrases used here carry the same implication without the statement. Calvin (reformed) reaches the same conclusion by the same route, and adds that God does not merely decide for the Manassites but approves their appeal, since they claimed only what could not be alienated without breaking his own decree.

The ruling has two halves, and Henry balances them. The daughters are tied to no particular husbands, there being choice enough within their father’s family, and he draws a rule from the liberty: children must not marry against their parents’ minds, and parents must consult their children’s affections and not force them on someone they cannot love, since forced marriages are not likely to prove blessings. But they are confined to their own kindred, so the portion stays where the lot put it; and since the lot was the LORD’s disposal, what men cannot improve they should not alter. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) puts the balance in a sentence: latitude enough, and a salutary restraint against a vexatious mixture of property. How narrow the restraint is, the witnesses dispute. Keil (grammatical-historical) reads it as the father’s tribe, so the husband must be a Manassite; Henry and Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) narrow it to the family within the tribe, Wesley arguing from the reason of the law, that God would keep families as well as tribes entire.

How far the law reaches is the sharper question. Keil observes that what begins as a ruling for five women is extended in the following verses into a general law for every heiress, and Gill (reformed) says the same of the clause about tribe to tribe. Gill also reports and rejects a Jewish limitation, that the order bound only Zelophehad’s daughters or held only until the land was divided: since the reason of the law continues afterwards, so must the law. Clarke and Wesley limit it from the other side. It touched none but heiresses, all other women being free; priests and Levites, having no inheritance, fell outside it, which is why the record shows them marrying into other tribes, and a commentator Clarke quotes builds on those marriages a possible kinship between Elisabeth and Mary at Luke 1:5. Wesley adds that a daughter with brothers was free to marry anywhere, though the inheritance would revert to her father’s kindred if they died.

Calvin marks the same boundary as a rule of interpretation. The words look wider than the case, and could be read as forbidding any man to marry outside his kindred; but the meaning of a law is to be sought from the occasion that produced it, and this one forbids mixed marriage only so far as it confounds hereditary right. The corollary is that a woman who gave up her paternal inheritance remained free to marry where she pleased. On why God should care so much, Henry answers from good order: estates would be entangled and genealogies perplexed, and one tribe grow rich by impoverishing another. Wesley answers from prophecy, that the family from which the Messiah was to come had to be beyond question. Gill closes by returning to the jubilee, which was meant to keep inheritances from moving between tribes but, as this case shows, could not do it without the present law.
10:
The execution is reported in a sentence, and the witnesses spend their attention on its details. Gill (reformed) notes that the five names appear here in a slightly different order from the earlier lists, Tirzah and Noah changing places, and reports two Jewish explanations without choosing between them: that the earlier order follows their birth and this one their marriages, or that the variation is deliberate, showing the sisters equal so that none is preferred. On the following verse he passes on a grammatical observation of the same kind. They were married into the families of Manasseh, in the plural, which is taken as a sign that their husbands were not all sons of one uncle but of several, though all within the kindred. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) adds nothing to the names here, referring back to his treatment of them at Numbers 27.

Ellicott (grammatical-historical) raises the one question of substance. Their father’s brothers’ sons would ordinarily mean first cousins, and he prefers to render it more loosely as the sons of their near kinsmen, since the Hebrew word generally denotes an uncle on the father’s side and probably does so here, but is used at Jeremiah 32:12 of a cousin. The difference is not academic: on the narrower reading the five women married into a single set of first cousins, on the wider one into a kin group of some extent. Gill’s note about the plural families pulls the same way, toward a group rather than a household. What no witness disputes is the outcome the chapter was written for, that the inheritance remained in the tribe of the family of their father.

Clarke draws the moral of the case from a commentator he quotes: by this example and the whole law of inheritance in the land, God’s people are taught to hold fast their inheritance in his promises and their right in Christ, which they hold by faith, keeping to the end the grace by which the Father made them meet to share the inheritance of the saints in light at Colossians 1:12. It is the only place in the chapter where the land settlement is read straight through to a spiritual inheritance, and it comes at the point where the narrative closes and the arrangement is shown to have worked.

The closing formula then ends more than the chapter. Keil (grammatical-historical) argues that it covers not only the laws of the preceding section but the whole body given in the plains of Moab, and so closes the book, setting the lawgiving there beside the lawgiving at Sinai which Leviticus 26:46 concludes in the same way. He is careful about what that does not prove: a formal close here implies nothing against the Mosaic origin of the explanation and enforcement of the law that follows in the next book. Gill keeps to the content, taking the commandments and judgments as the judicial laws about the division of the land, the case of inheritances and the cities of refuge, and fixing the place as the plains of Moab where Israel had lain since Balak first watched them. Henry (puritan-evangelical) observes that most of these laws bear on the settlement the people were now entering, and turns that forward: whatever new condition providence brings us into, we must ask God to teach us its duties and enable us to do them, doing the work of the day in its day and the duty of a place in its place. Clarke closes the book at length and with feeling, on the union in every transaction of God’s holiness and justice with his benevolence and mercy, and on the reader standing where Israel stood, in the plains of Moab with only Jordan between him and the promised inheritance.
